tagline: The rota on everyone's phone, with swaps that sort themselves out.
verdictSummary: Two dollars fifty a head is priced against the effort of not doing it, and the software underneath is a weekend. The gap is adoption: this only works if every member of staff has it on their phone and opens it, and an installed app with push notifications is a different thing from a web page they have to remember. Nothing here is a network or a dataset, so kinda is right.
coreLoopDIY: Publish the rota once and let it maintain itself: staff see their shifts, offer them up, and pick up cover, with your approval as the only step that needs you.
whatYouLose: the mobile apps and push notifications
the time clock and its payroll export on the paid tiers
availability requests handled entirely in-app by staff
somebody else keeping it up on a Friday night
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the whole value is that the rota reaches everyone and changes reach them too, and that requires an app people already have rather than a link you keep resending.
prompt:
Build a scheduling tool whose distinguishing feature is that shift changes resolve without you.

Stack: your choice, Postgres, Docker Compose, a domain with TLS. Mobile-first, keyboard-free, usable on a slow connection.

Schedule: employees with roles and stated availability, shifts with role, start, end and required headcount, published a week at a time.

Availability: each employee sets recurring availability and one-off exceptions. Assigning someone outside their availability is allowed but warns and records that it was overridden — a hard block just gets worked around by text message.

The self-service loop, which is the point:
- **Offer a shift up**: an employee releases a shift into an open pool.
- **Claim from the pool**: anyone with the right role and matching availability sees it and can claim. Claiming is atomic — two people tapping at the same second must not both get it, and this needs a real transaction, not a check-then-write.
- **Direct swap**: propose a trade with a named colleague, who accepts or declines.
- Every resolution needs one manager approval and nothing else. The manager sees a single queue of pending changes with accept and reject.
- Rules enforced before a claim is offered: not already working that time, not exceeding a weekly hours cap, and a minimum rest gap between shifts.

Notifications: web push where available, email otherwise, for published schedules, changes to your own shifts, and a shift available in the pool you qualify for. Be honest in the README that without a native app this is where a self-hosted version is weakest.

Show, on the schedule, the coverage per role per hour as a small bar, so an understaffed Saturday is visible while it is still a draft.

Write tests for atomic claiming under concurrency, for the rest-gap and weekly-cap rules blocking a claim, and for availability overrides being recorded.

Do not build a time clock, payroll, or multi-location support.

faq.a: Because two people claiming the same shift is a guaranteed argument, and a naive check-then-write gets it wrong exactly when the pool is busy. One transaction with a conditional update solves it and needs a test to stay solved.

faq.q: Why warn rather than block on availability?
faq.a: Because managers legitimately need to ask someone to work outside their stated availability, and a hard block pushes that conversation into text messages where the schedule cannot see it. Warning and recording keeps it in the system.

faq.q: How much does the lack of an app really cost?
faq.a: A lot, honestly. Hourly staff will not check a web page, and web push is inconsistent on iOS. Expect to also send an SMS for anything urgent, which is a real cost the subscription absorbs.

faq.q: What does When I Work cost?
faq.a: $2.50 per user per month for a single location, $5 for multi-location, $8 for the top tier — with the time clock and payroll export on the higher tiers rather than the entry one.
